title: Inherited Cancer Genes: MSI and Lynch, RET and MEN 2, BRCA1/2
summary: Read an MSI-high result as a Lynch screen rather than a diagnosis, match RET codons to the age of prophylactic thyroidectomy, and interpret BRCA1/BRCA2 breast and ovarian risk figures as study-dependent estimates.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 78 High-Yield Hits 4 (MSI-H ≥2 of 5 markers → Lynch workup and immunotherapy), 7 (RET codon 918 in MEN 2B, codon 634 in MEN 2A) and 12 (BRCA1/BRCA2 breast and ovarian risk by age 70). Checked against Gallon 2021 (Lynch screening guideline review), Li 2020 (MSI review; used only for the NCI panel and the MSI-H/MSI-L definitions), the 2015 revised ATA medullary thyroid carcinoma guideline (Wells 2015; read via a page-fetch tool, first 200,000 of about 468,000 characters), Raue 2018 (MEN 2 review), Kim 2021 (MTC guideline review) and Levy-Lahad 2007 (BRCA cancer risks). Qualifications taught: MSI-H is a screen, and sporadic MSI-H tumours (MLH1 promoter methylation, BRAF V600E) are sorted out before germline testing; mixed NCI panels can miss MSH6 deficiency; codon 634 is the classical MEN 2A codon, but routine sequencing now finds more moderate-risk mutations; M918T is about 95% (ATA) or >95% (Raue) of MEN 2B; BRCA risks are taught as the meta-analysis figures with their study-design dependence. Not taught: the reviewer’s mention of LOH in the MSI-H definition. The revised Bethesda guideline (Umar 2004) page on PMC returned a reCAPTCHA check and was not read.

objectives: Define MSI-H on the five-marker NCI panel and explain why mononucleotide panels or four-protein MMR immunohistochemistry are now preferred.
Describe the Lynch screening pipeline: MMR-deficient tumour, then BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter methylation, then germline MMR testing.
Match RET M918T, C634/A883F and moderate-risk codons to the ATA timing of prophylactic thyroidectomy.
State the meta-analysis breast and ovarian cancer risks by age 70 for BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers and why published estimates differ.

scenes.title: Three results, three families
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three results reach the genetics clinic. (1) Colon cancer, 58 years: tumour MSI-high. (2) Newborn whose father has MEN 2B: germline RET M918T. (3) Woman, 35 years: germline BRCA2 pathogenic variant. Question token: “Which result is a screen, and which sets a date?”

cues.text: Three results reach the genetics clinic. A colon cancer in a fifty-eight-year-old is reported as microsatellite instability high.
A newborn whose father has MEN 2B carries the RET M918T mutation. And a thirty-five-year-old woman carries a BRCA2 pathogenic variant.
Which result is only a screen, and which one sets a date for surgery?

scenes.title: Germline variant, tumour clue
scenes.altText: Three cards. Lynch syndrome: a germline pathogenic variant in one of four mismatch repair (MMR) genes, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 (EPCAM 3′ deletions silence MSH2); nearly all Lynch colorectal cancers are MMR-deficient after the second allele is lost; Lynch ≈ 3% of colorectal and endometrial cancers. MEN2: autosomal dominant, gain-of-function missense RET mutations; medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) ± pheochromocytoma, hyperparathyroidism. BRCA1/BRCA2: carriers have breast and ovarian cancer risks high enough to warrant risk-reducing surgery.

cues.text: Lynch syndrome is a germline pathogenic variant in one of four mismatch repair genes: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2. Deletions at the end of EPCAM also silence MSH2. Lynch accounts for about three percent of colorectal and endometrial cancers.

In a Lynch carrier, the tumour loses the second copy of the gene, so nearly all Lynch colorectal cancers are mismatch repair deficient. That deficiency leaves a clue in the tumour: microsatellite instability.

MEN 2 is autosomal dominant and caused by gain-of-function missense mutations in the RET proto-oncogene. It is highly penetrant for medullary thyroid carcinoma, sometimes with pheochromocytoma or hyperparathyroidism.
BRCA1 and BRCA2 pathogenic variants raise breast and ovarian cancer risk enough to warrant risk-reducing surgery, although the exact risk figures vary between studies.

props.title: BRCA1 / BRCA2 (germline)
lines: Breast + ovarian risk high enough for risk-reducing surgery

scenes.title: MSI-high: a screen, not a diagnosis
scenes.altText: Left card: NCI reference panel = 2 mononucleotide (BAT-25, BAT-26) + 3 dinucleotide (D2S123, D5S346, D17S250) markers; instability at ≥2 markers = MSI-H, at 1 = MSI-L. Mixed panels misclassified many MSH6-deficient tumours as MSS/MSI-L; panels of five mononucleotide markers classify 97.7–100% of MSH6-deficient tumours as MSI-H. Alternative: immunohistochemistry for all four MMR proteins. Right card, screening pipeline: MMR-deficient tumour → test BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter methylation (both associated with sporadic tumours) → only if both absent → germline MMR testing. ≈ 15% of colorectal cancers are MSI-H, Lynch ≈ 3%. Bottom token: pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) — first site-agnostic licence, based on tumour MMR deficiency.

cues.text: The original National Cancer Institute panel used two mononucleotide markers, BAT-25 and BAT-26, and three dinucleotide markers. Instability at two or more of the five is MSI-high; at only one, MSI-low.

Mixed panels often called MSH6-deficient tumours stable or MSI-low, so labs moved to panels of five mononucleotide markers. Immunohistochemistry for all four mismatch repair proteins is the other screening method.

About fifteen percent of colorectal cancers are MSI-high, but Lynch causes only about three percent. Sporadic MSI-high tumours are linked to MLH1 promoter methylation and BRAF V600E, so a deficient tumour is tested for both, and only if both are absent is germline testing selected.

Mismatch repair deficiency also predicts immunotherapy benefit. Pembrolizumab, an anti-PD-1 antibody, was the first cancer drug licensed regardless of tumour site, based only on tumour mismatch repair deficiency.

scenes.title: RET sets the date; BRCA sets the odds
scenes.altText: Left card (2015 revised ATA medullary thyroid carcinoma guideline): ATA-highest risk = MEN 2B, RET M918T (exon 16; ≈ 95% of MEN 2B in the guideline, > 95% in a 2018 review) → thyroidectomy in the first year of life; ATA-high = C634 (exon 11, the classical MEN 2A codon) and A883F → thyroidectomy at age 5 or earlier if calcitonin rises; ATA-moderate = other codons → timing by rising calcitonin; pheochromocytoma screening by age 11 (high/highest) or 16 (moderate). Note: routine sequencing now finds more moderate-risk exon 13–15 mutations. Right card, BRCA risk by age 70 (meta-analysis of case-based studies): BRCA1 breast 65%, ovarian 39%; BRCA2 breast 45%, ovarian 11%; higher in multiple-case family studies. Hook answers card.

cues.text: The American Thyroid Association groups RET mutations by risk. Highest risk is MEN 2B with M918T in exon sixteen, found in about ninety-five percent of MEN 2B. These children should have a thyroidectomy in the first year of life.

High risk is codon 634, the classic MEN 2A mutation, and A883F: thyroidectomy at age five, or earlier if calcitonin rises. Moderate-risk codons are timed by a rising calcitonin. With routine sequencing, moderate-risk mutations are now found more often.

For BRCA, a meta-analysis of case-based studies estimated risk by age seventy at sixty-five percent for breast and thirty-nine percent for ovarian cancer in BRCA1 carriers, and forty-five and eleven percent in BRCA2 carriers. Studies of high-risk families gave higher figures.

Back to the hook. MSI-high is a screen that needs BRAF and MLH1 methylation results before germline testing. RET M918T sets a date: surgery in the first year. BRCA2 sets the odds for surveillance and risk-reducing surgery.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 1 MSI-H: screen → BRAF, MLH1 methylation, then germline
2 RET M918T: thyroidectomy in first year
3 BRCA2: risk estimate → surveillance, surgery options

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “MSI-high colon cancer means Lynch syndrome” (✓ screen — most MSI-H colorectal cancers are sporadic; check BRAF V600E and MLH1 methylation first); “Stable on the old 5-marker panel rules out MMR deficiency” (✓ mixed panels can miss MSH6 loss; use mononucleotide panel or four-protein IHC); “MEN 2A codon 634 and MEN 2B M918T get the same surgery timing” (✓ M918T first year; C634 by age 5).

cues.text: Trap one: MSI-high colon cancer means Lynch syndrome. No: it is a screen. Most MSI-high colorectal cancers are sporadic, so check BRAF V600E and MLH1 methylation first.
Trap two: a stable result on the old five-marker panel rules out mismatch repair deficiency. No: mixed panels can miss MSH6 loss. Use a mononucleotide panel or four-protein immunohistochemistry.
Trap three: codon 634 and codon 918 get the same surgery timing. No: M918T means thyroidectomy in the first year of life; codon 634 by age five.

props.title: ✗ “MSI-high colon cancer = Lynch.”

props.title: ✗ “Stable on old 5-marker panel = MMR intact.”

props.title: ✗ “634 and 918: same surgery age.”

scenes.title: Flags, dates and odds
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “MSI raises a flag, RET sets a date, BRCA sets the odds.” Tokens: MSI-H → flag (screen, then sort sporadic) · RET → date (918 first year, 634 by five) · BRCA → odds (BRCA1 > BRCA2 for ovary). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: MSI raises a flag, RET sets a date, BRCA sets the odds. A flag needs follow-up, a RET codon sets the surgery age, and a BRCA variant gives a risk estimate.

Where it breaks: moderate-risk RET codons have no fixed date, because calcitonin decides. BRCA odds are averages that vary by study design and family history. And a negative MSI flag on an old mixed panel can still miss MSH6 deficiency.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “MSI-high: screen → BRAF V600E, MLH1 methylation → germline” and “RET M918T: first year · C634: by age 5 · BRCA: risk estimate”.

cues.text: Treat an MSI-high tumour as a screen that needs BRAF and MLH1 methylation results before germline testing, let the RET codon set the thyroidectomy age, and read BRCA figures as study-dependent risk estimates.

props.label: MSI-high: screen → BRAF V600E, MLH1 methylation → germline
RET M918T: first year · C634: by age 5 · BRCA: risk estimate

explanation.what: Plain language: some families carry an inherited change in one gene that raises cancer risk. A tumour test can raise a flag that such a change may be present, and a confirmed inherited change can set the timing of preventive surgery or screening. Scientific terms: germline pathogenic variant, mismatch repair (MMR: MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2; EPCAM deletion), microsatellite instability (MSI-H, MSI-L, MSS), immunohistochemistry (IHC), MLH1 promoter methylation, BRAF V600E, RET proto-oncogene, MEN 2A/2B, ATA risk categories, calcitonin, BRCA1/BRCA2 penetrance.
explanation.why: Lynch tumours lose the second MMR allele, so nearly all Lynch colorectal cancers are MMR-deficient and unstable at microsatellites; but sporadic tumours can silence MLH1 by promoter methylation, so MSI-H alone does not prove an inherited variant. MSH2–MSH6 maintains only mononucleotide repeats, so panels weighted to dinucleotide repeats can miss MSH6 loss. RET mutations are gain-of-function, and the codon predicts how early medullary thyroid carcinoma develops.
explanation.measure: NCI panel: BAT-25, BAT-26, D2S123, D5S346, D17S250; ≥2 unstable = MSI-H, 1 = MSI-L. Mononucleotide panels call 97.7–100% of MSH6-deficient tumours MSI-H. ≈15% of colorectal cancers MSI-H; Lynch ≈3% of colorectal and endometrial cancers. RET: M918T ≈95% (ATA) / >95% (Raue) of MEN 2B → thyroidectomy in the first year; C634, A883F → by age 5 (earlier if calcitonin rises); moderate → by rising calcitonin; pheochromocytoma screening by age 11 (high/highest) or 16 (moderate). BRCA by age 70 (Antoniou meta-analysis as reported by Levy-Lahad 2007): BRCA1 breast 65%, ovarian 39%; BRCA2 breast 45%, ovarian 11%; family-based BCLC estimates higher (BRCA1 breast 71%, BRCA2 breast 84%).
explanation.differs: MSI by PCR (DNA instability; mononucleotide panel) vs MMR IHC (protein loss; stain all four); sporadic MSI-H (MLH1 methylation, BRAF V600E) vs Lynch (germline MMR variant); ATA-highest (M918T) vs ATA-high (C634, A883F) vs ATA-moderate; BRCA1 vs BRCA2 (BRCA1 higher ovarian risk).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the MSI-H cut-off on the five-marker panel, the next test after an MSI-H or MLH1-deficient colorectal cancer, the RET codon that means the earliest thyroidectomy, and which BRCA gene carries the higher ovarian cancer risk.

mnemonic.text: MSI raises a flag, RET sets a date, BRCA sets the odds.
mnemonic.explanation: An MSI-H result needs follow-up testing; the RET codon sets the age of prophylactic thyroidectomy; a BRCA variant gives a risk estimate for surveillance and risk-reducing surgery.
mnemonic.limitation: Moderate-risk RET codons have no fixed date (rising calcitonin decides); BRCA odds are population averages that vary with study design and family history; and a stable result on an old mixed-marker panel can still miss MSH6 deficiency.

analogyLimitations: Flag, date and odds are memory labels, not clinical rules; management follows the guideline and the clinical team.
Risk figures vary by population and study design; the numbers are from the cited sources.
takeaway: Treat an MSI-high tumour as a screen that needs BRAF and MLH1 methylation results before germline testing, let the RET codon set the thyroidectomy age, and read BRCA figures as study-dependent risk estimates.

questions.stem: A colorectal cancer is MSI-high on a five-marker PCR panel. Immunohistochemistry shows loss of MLH1 and PMS2, and the tumour carries BRAF V600E. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The tumour is most likely sporadic; BRAF V600E points away from Lynch syndrome
options.rationale: Correct. BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter methylation are associated with sporadic MMR-deficient tumours, and screening pipelines send only tumours lacking both for germline MMR testing.

options.text: Lynch syndrome is confirmed by the MSI-high result
options.rationale: Incorrect. MSI-H is a screen: about 15% of colorectal cancers are MSI-H, while Lynch causes about 3%.

options.text: PMS2 loss proves a germline PMS2 variant
options.rationale: Incorrect. PMS2 is degraded when it cannot pair with functional MLH1, so PMS2 loss alongside MLH1 loss does not by itself indicate a PMS2 variant.

options.text: MSI-high status excludes the patient from immunotherapy
options.rationale: Incorrect. MMR deficiency predicts benefit from the anti-PD-1 antibody pembrolizumab, which is licensed regardless of tumour site in MMR-deficient cancers.

questions.stem: A newborn whose father has MEN 2B tests positive for germline RET M918T. Under the 2015 revised ATA guideline, when should thyroidectomy be performed?

options.text: In the first year of life
options.rationale: Correct. M918T is the ATA-highest-risk mutation, and these children should have thyroidectomy in the first year of life.
Incorrect. Age 5 (or earlier if calcitonin rises) is the timing for the ATA-high category, C634 and A883F.

options.text: Only when serum calcitonin becomes elevated
options.rationale: Incorrect. Calcitonin-guided timing applies to the ATA-moderate category.
Incorrect. Age 11 is when pheochromocytoma screening should begin in the high and highest categories, not the surgery age.

questions.stem: In the meta-analysis of case-based studies reported by Levy-Lahad and Friedman (2007), how did ovarian cancer risk by age 70 compare between BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers?

options.text: Higher in BRCA1 carriers (about 39%) than in BRCA2 carriers (about 11%)
options.rationale: Correct. The meta-analysis estimated ovarian cancer risk by age 70 at 39% for BRCA1 and 11% for BRCA2.

options.text: Higher in BRCA2 carriers than in BRCA1 carriers
options.rationale: Incorrect. BRCA2 carriers had the lower ovarian risk (11% vs 39%).
Incorrect. 65% was the BRCA1 breast cancer estimate, not the ovarian estimate.

options.text: Not raised above the general population
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both genes raise ovarian cancer risk substantially; the review describes risks high enough to warrant risk-reducing surgery.

claims.text: Lynch = germline MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 variant (EPCAM deletions silence MSH2); ≈3% of colorectal and endometrial cancers; nearly all Lynch colorectal cancers are MMR-deficient after the second hit.
NCI panel (BAT-25, BAT-26 + three dinucleotide markers); ≥2 unstable = MSI-H, 1 = MSI-L; mixed panels miss MSH6 deficiency; mononucleotide panels and four-protein IHC preferred.
≈15% of colorectal cancers MSI-H; MMR-deficient tumours tested for BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter methylation; germline testing if both absent; PMS2 degraded without functional MLH1.
Pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) first site-agnostic licence based on tumour MMR deficiency.
MEN 2 autosomal dominant, gain-of-function RET; M918T ≈95% (ATA) / >95% (Raue) of MEN 2B; C634 classical MEN 2A codon; routine sequencing finds more moderate-risk mutations.
Thyroidectomy: M918T first year; C634/A883F at age 5 or earlier if calcitonin rises; moderate by rising calcitonin; pheochromocytoma screening by 11 (H/HST) or 16 (MOD).
By age 70 (meta-analysis): BRCA1 breast 65%, ovarian 39%; BRCA2 breast 45%, ovarian 11%; family-based estimates higher; risks warrant risk-reducing surgery.
Reviewer wording: MSI-H defined as “instability/LOH” in ≥2 of 5 markers.
claims.note: The LOH part of the definition was not found in the sources read; not taught.

claims.text: “MSI raises a flag, RET sets a date, BRCA sets the odds.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 78 Hit 4 says MSI-H (≥2 of 5 markers) leads to Lynch syndrome workup without noting that MSI-H is a screen: about 15% of colorectal cancers are MSI-H while Lynch causes about 3%, and current pipelines test MMR-deficient tumours for BRAF V600E and MLH1 promoter methylation (associated with sporadic tumours) before germline testing (Gallon 2021) (register flag rv-ch78-msi-screen-sporadic).

Ch. 78 Hit 4 defines MSI-H on the five-marker panel without noting that the mixed NCI panel (two mononucleotide, three dinucleotide markers) misclassified many MSH6-deficient tumours as MSS/MSI-L; mononucleotide-only panels or four-protein MMR immunohistochemistry are now used (Gallon 2021) (register flag rv-ch78-msi-screen-sporadic).

Ch. 78 Hit 7 calls codon 634 the most common MEN 2A mutation. Raue 2018 describes 634 as the classical high-risk codon that was previously the most common, and reports that routine RET sequencing of all MTC patients now detects more moderate-risk exon 13–15 mutations; the ATA 2015 guideline (portion read) gives M918T as about 95% of MEN 2B (reviewer >95%) (register flag rv-ch78-ret-634-frequency).
